1.pericope_label: The song of songs, which is Solomon’s

schools.summary: Henry divides the title into the nature, dignity and penman of the book, holding that a song is the fit form because the design is to stir and heat the affections, that this one excels the other scripture songs as having more of Christ in it, and that it is not the song of fools, as many songs of love are, but the song of the wisest of men.

Gill takes the title as a Hebrew superlative on the pattern of the Holy of holies, gives the book to Solomon as amanuensis of the Holy Ghost against the Jewish tradition that assigns it to a later king and his men, and reports a saying that wherever the name of Solomon occurs in this song the Holy One is meant.

Clarke defines ode, idyl, pastoral and marriage-song and finds the book falls under none of them but is most like a mask written for a wedding, lists six opinions held about its meaning, argues from the absence of the name of God and the silence of the New Testament that it is not an allegory of Christ and the church, names the interpreters he refuses among them Gill, and reports that after nearly fifty years of reading he sees nothing of Christ in it; Wesley takes the superlative of author, subject and matter, and says the subject is not Solomon but a greater than Solomon.

Keil and Delitzsch call the Song the most obscure book of the Old Testament, since inexplicable passages remain on any principle of interpretation, and report that its canonicity was doubted in the Jewish schools of the first century until the love-poem was taken as spiritual and read allegorically, as the Targum read it of the history of a nation from the Exodus to the coming of Messiah; Ellicott settles the title by grammar, since the article on the second word makes it the surpassing song rather than one song out of a thousand and five, and refers the authorship elsewhere.

debates: Is the Song an allegory at all? Keil and Delitzsch report the allegorical reading as the answer that saved the book for the canon, and the Targum as its earliest example. Gill, Henry and Wesley write throughout as though the question were settled, the bridegroom being Christ and the bride the church. Clarke refuses the whole scheme: he lists six opinions, denies that antiquity or great names settle anything, argues from the absence of the name of God in the book and from its never being quoted in the New Testament, names the interpreters he is opposing, and says that after nearly fifty years of reading he sees in it nothing of Christ and his church.
outliers: Clarke names Gill among the interpreters he is refusing, so that two of the voices in this set are in direct and open disagreement with each other.

Clarke dates the book from the numbers in it, arguing that it cannot be the work of old age since the writer then had seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines while the Song names sixty and eighty.
Keil and Delitzsch admit at the outset that interpreting the book is an ungrateful task, since an interpreter is thanked for the separate parts only if his conception of the whole is approved.
Clarke suggests that an English poet took the idea of his mask from this book, having decided that the Song is neither ode nor idyl nor pastoral but a wedding entertainment of its own kind.
themes: a title that is a superlative
the most obscure book of the canon
six opinions and no revelation to decide them
a commentator who names his opponents
fifty years of reading and no allegory found

2.pericope_label: Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth: thy name is as ointment poured forth: draw me, we will run after thee

schools.summary: Henry compares the unnamed him to the woman at the sepulchre who said, if thou have borne him hence, and observes that those full of Christ think others must be so too; he reads the drawing of the fourth verse as doctrine, that we are naturally backward and must pray for the grace by which the unwilling are made willing, yet are not driven to Christ but drawn in a way agreeable to rational creatures.

Gill calls the opening a relative without an antecedent, the antecedent being only in the speaker’s mind, keeps the ointments to the custom by which lovers anointed themselves and commended each other’s perfumes, and reports an interpreter who gives the words of the fourth verse to the virgins rather than to the bride.

Clarke explains the third person as modesty and takes the virgins of the third verse to mean the speaker herself, reports that the versions generally read thy breasts and that the two are said to stand for the Old and New Testaments, and reads the fourth verse plainly, that her spouse is a potentate and no ordinary person; Wesley defends the abrupt opening as proper to writing of this kind, citing Homer and Virgil, and draws from the change of number the lesson that the spouse is one body of many members.

Keil and Delitzsch trace the reading thy breasts to a defectively written word, refuse the proposed let him give me to drink since to give to drink with kisses is unsupported, take the opening word as partitive so that the speaker is one among many, dispute with three interpreters over whether the word in the third verse means smell given off or the sense of smell, and hold that the accents require draw me, so will we run after thee; Ellicott condemns the breasts reading because the words are spoken by a woman and not to one, quotes an English lyric for the variant about drinking, divides the third verse into three clauses, and reads the king of the fourth verse as a supposition.

debates: What stands in the text of the second verse? Keil and Delitzsch and Clarke both report that the Greek and the versions generally read thy breasts where the English has thy love, the difference being one defectively written word; Clarke adds that the two are taken to represent the Old and New Testaments, and Ellicott calls that the origin of many fanciful interpretations before condemning the reading outright, since the words are spoken by a woman and not to one. A second proposal, let him give me to drink for let him kiss me, is granted by Ellicott to preserve the metaphor of the wine and refused by Keil and Delitzsch as an unsupported expression.
outliers: Ellicott answers a Hebrew variant with an English lyric, quoting the lines about leaving a kiss in the cup and asking for no wine.
Keil and Delitzsch take the first word as a partitive, so that the speaker of the opening line is only one of the many among whom the kisses are distributed.
Ellicott reports without softening it that those who take the king for the object of these verses understand the virgins of the third verse as the ladies of his harem.
Wesley defends the abrupt opening by the practice of the epic poets, where what happened first is brought in as though accidentally after much else.
themes: a pronoun with no antecedent
thy love or thy breasts
a kiss left in the cup
oil and name at play in one sound
drawn, not driven

5.pericope_label: I am black, but comely, O ye daughters of Jerusalem: look not upon me, because I am black: tell me, O thou whom my soul loveth, where thou feedest

schools.summary: Henry takes the title of the seventh verse, the one whom my soul loveth, for the undoubted character of every true believer, marking both the sincerity and the strength of their love, and finds in the verse that Christ provides both repast and repose for his sheep, who are not scattered on the mountains but fed together.

Gill divides black and comely between two views of the speaker, black in herself and in the eyes of the world, comely in the eyes of Christ, reads the warning not to look on her as a caution against being stumbled by her sufferings, and cites a father for the claim that the maxim about knowing oneself was not first the oracle’s, since Solomon had it before and had it from Moses.

Clarke explains the blackness by climate and by the tanned cloth of the tents, reports that the women of the city are said to stand for the synagogue and the bride for the church before remarking that it is easy to find spiritual meanings since every creed will furnish them, sets the jealousy of the sixth verse in the politics of a foreign marriage, and suggests that the festival included something like our masks, citing an English poem of that kind and a Latin eclogue on shepherds singing at noon; Wesley refers the blackness to the complexion of the foreign princess, allegorises the mother’s children into false brethren and false teachers, and reads the noon as the time of persecution.

Keil and Delitzsch infer from the address that the speaker came from another district and note, in the interest of the mystical interpretation, that the first congregations of the church were from the same one; they make the colour word a diminutive meaning blackish, and add that a face judged not beautiful is judged otherwise as soon as its owner speaks; Ellicott calls the comparison playful raillery redeemed by a compliment, argues that the accidental sunburn cannot prove the speaker a foreign princess, rejects three proposed senses of the veiled of the seventh verse in favour of a wandering got by transposing two letters, and quotes a rabbinic exposition as an instance of the fanciful treatment the book has received.

debates: Was the bride a foreign princess? Clarke assumes it and explains the jealousy of the sixth verse as the resentment of the women of the country at a king who went abroad for a wife; Wesley refers the blackness to that princess’s complexion. Ellicott turns the same verse the other way, since a darkness got by working in the sun is accidental and therefore proves nothing about her birth, and he reports that many who hold the dramatic theory read the eighth verse as the court ladies mocking her low birth. Keil and Delitzsch place her in another district altogether.
outliers: Clarke reports the allegorical reading of the fifth verse and dismisses it in a sentence, that it is easy to find spiritual meanings since every creed will furnish them.
Ellicott quotes a rabbinic exposition of the seventh verse at length as a specimen of the fanciful treatment this book has received.

Keil and Delitzsch note, while identifying the speaker’s home district, that the first congregations of the church came from the same district, a remark they say they make in the interest of the mystical interpretation.
Wesley alone allegorises the angry brothers of the sixth verse, making them false brethren and false teachers who leave the church no time for her own vineyard.
themes: black by the sun, comely by grace
a spiritual meaning for every creed
a complexion that proves nothing
shepherds sheltering at midday
veiled, wandering, or blindfold

9.pericope_label: I have compared thee, O my love, to a company of horses in Pharaoh’s chariots: thy cheeks are comely with rows of jewels: we will make thee borders of gold

schools.summary: Henry keeps the ornaments as figures of grace, holding that the gifts Christ bestows are many and depend on each other and that he who is the Author of the work will be its Finisher, and adds the caution that it is Christ himself and not his gifts who is precious to believers.

Gill glosses the address as the names used between lovers and notes that the Greek has my neighbour, takes the ornaments of the tenth verse as turtledoves after the Greek and reconstructs them as an earring hung from a plate across the forehead down both cheeks with a jewel falling to the nose, identifying it with what was put on the patriarch’s bride at the well, and hears in the plural of the eleventh verse Christ speaking in his own name and in the name of the other two divine Persons.

Clarke renders the ninth verse to my mare and explains that mares were preferred in the East as swifter and hardier, defends the comparison with a Greek idyl in which the most beautiful woman of antiquity is likened to a horse in a chariot, and quotes a traveller on the pearls, gold chains and strung coins worn by Arabian women, adding that one of their ornamented scent bottles lies before him as he writes; Wesley makes the likeness one of strength and courage, since the church is terrible to her enemies, and takes the plural of the eleventh verse for the Son and the Father.

Keil and Delitzsch use the ninth verse to stage the scene, bringing Solomon on for the first time and noting that the woman has been alone with the ladies of the palace, who remain but out of hearing, and that his word for her is one of friendship since she is not yet his bride; Ellicott defends the equine comparison from three poets and from the taste of an Arab chief, rules out the supposition of a gift between monarchs, derives the words for the ornaments from roots meaning to go round and to perforate, quotes travellers on the coins and pearls worn about the face, and answers the dramatic reading of the eleventh verse by observing that no theory is needed to explain a lover wishing to adorn his beloved.

debates: Can a woman be compared to a horse? Clarke and Ellicott both treat the comparison as needing defence, Clarke answering with a Greek idyl that likens the most beautiful woman of antiquity to a horse in a chariot, Ellicott with three poets who did the same and with the observation that an Arab chief would prefer the points of his horse to the charms of his mistress; Ellicott also reports those who, being offended, suppose that only the trappings of the royal equipage are meant. Wesley avoids the question by making the likeness one of strength and courage, and Gill by passing to the address.
outliers: Clarke reports that he has seen the ornamented scent bottles he is describing and that one of them lies before him as he writes.
Ellicott gathers three travellers on the ornaments of the tenth verse, including an English lady’s description of a sultana wearing four strings of great pearls.

Ellicott states the dramatic reading of the eleventh verse, in which the offer of richer ornaments is a bid to dazzle a rustic girl, and answers that no theory is needed to explain a lover wishing to adorn his beloved.
Keil and Delitzsch treat the ninth verse as a stage direction, bringing the king on for the first time and leaving the ladies of the palace present but out of hearing.
themes: a mare in the chariots
poets who praised women as horses
coins strung across the forehead
ornaments read as ordinances
the giver above the gift

12.pericope_label: While the king sitteth at his table, my spikenard sendeth forth the smell thereof: a bundle of myrrh is my wellbeloved unto me: my beloved is as a cluster of camphire

schools.summary: Henry spreads the royal table in the gospel, where the king sits to see his guests, to bid them welcome and to carve for them, and takes the whole passage as the mutual endearments of Christ and his church.

Gill takes the table for the round table of the ancients, describes the myrrh as the liquid sort carried in a bottle in the bosom as people carry smelling bottles, reports that some take the plant for sweet marjoram, and argues from a Roman naturalist and a historian that the place named was famous for palms and balsam, so that the clusters are dates and not what we call camphire, which does not grow in clusters and was unknown to the ancients.

Clarke renders the phrase of the twelfth verse in his circle, meaning the circle of friends at the festival or a round table, passes on another writer’s point that it is the bundle of myrrh and not the beloved that lies all night between the breasts, and offers his own guess at the cluster, that the poet means the dark hair which the Greeks compared to bunches of grapes; Wesley keeps to the custom of pouring ointments on the heads of guests and declines to settle what the plant of the fourteenth verse was.

Keil and Delitzsch object that most interpreters ignore the lessons of botany in explaining the thirteenth verse of a little bunch of myrrh, since the plant is an exotic there, its aromatic part is resin, and resin cannot be tied in a bunch; Ellicott refuses the scene in which the monarch retires to his banquet after failing to allure the shepherdess, traces the spikenard to an Indian plant of the valerian order, cites an early rabbinic code by way of a scholar for the wearing of myrrh bottles at the neck, quotes an English song about the necklace on the beloved’s breast, and identifies the cluster of the fourteenth verse with the henna of the Arabs on a traveller’s report from the one place where it grows.

debates: What is the cluster of the fourteenth verse? Ellicott identifies it confidently with the henna of the Arabs, on the report of a traveller who found it growing in abundance at that place, and rejects a writer who prefers a favourite kind of grape as giving no sufficient reason. Gill argues that the place was famous for palms and balsam and that Jewish writers therefore took the clusters for dates, and denies that what we call camphire can be meant at all, since it neither grows in clusters nor was known to the ancients. Clarke reports a proposal of a grape from a certain island and then guesses at dark clustering hair; Wesley declines the question as one we are not concerned to settle.
outliers: Ellicott sets beside the thirteenth verse an English song about wishing to be the necklace that rises and falls on the beloved and is scarcely unclasped at night.
Keil and Delitzsch charge most interpreters of the thirteenth verse with ignoring the lessons of botany, since the aromatic part of myrrh is a resin that cannot be tied in a bunch.
Ellicott reports that the leaves of the plant he identifies are dried and pounded into a paste with which women of all ranks dye the palms of their hands and the soles of their feet.
Clarke passes on the observation that it is the bundle of myrrh, not the beloved, which is said to lie all night between the breasts.
themes: a king in his circle
myrrh that cannot be tied in a bunch
a necklace envied in an English song
henna, dates, or clustering hair
a question one voice declines

15.pericope_label: Behold, thou art fair, my love: thou hast doves’ eyes: also our bed is green: the beams of our house are cedar

schools.summary: Gill takes the opening word of the fifteenth verse as a note of attention, of admiration and of asseveration, calling her to consider her comeliness in Christ rather than her own blackness; reads the answering verse as her giving the commendation back, his fairness being essential and hers derived; and turns the house of the last verse into the congregation, its beams the ministers and members who support it.

Clarke identifies the dove as the large and beautiful bird of the country, takes the bed for a green bank on which they sat while out on a walk, supposes the beams to be a cedar interwoven with a tree of the cypress kind making a natural bower, and closes the chapter with the note that the first day of the marriage ceremonies is supposed to end here; Wesley makes the doves mild and faithful, sharpens the answering verse into thou and thou only art fair, and observes that cedar and cypress are alike strong and fragrant.

Keil and Delitzsch argue that the sixteenth verse must be her echo to the king, since otherwise the poet would have used a different demonstrative, and answer the scholar who reads the words as politeness distinguishing her true beloved from a king she cannot bear, replying that when a man and a woman address each other so it is as certainly an interchange as that one and one are two and not three; Ellicott notes that the fifteenth verse transfers the song to a male speaker whom the dramatic theory cannot identify since the poem gives no indication, counts seven of about fifty scriptural mentions of the dove within this short book, quotes two English poets on doves’ eyes, and derives the word for rafters from a root meaning to run.

debates: Who speaks the fifteenth verse, and to whom is the sixteenth addressed? Ellicott observes that the advocates of the dramatic theory cannot agree whether the male speaker is the king or the shepherd, and says the poem gives no indication and that the terms of endearment will not bear the weight of any theory. Keil and Delitzsch take the opposite view of the next verse and argue it from grammar, since a different demonstrative would have been required if she were answering another man; they reject outright the reading in which her words are politeness to a king she finds insufferable.
outliers: Ellicott counts the doves, finding seven of about fifty scriptural mentions of the bird within this one short book, and quotes two English poets on doves’ eyes.

Keil and Delitzsch settle the question of who is addressed with an arithmetical retort, that an exchange of such words between a man and a woman is as certainly an interchange of address as that one and one are two and not three.
Clarke ends his comment with a stage direction, that the first day of the marriage ceremonies is supposed to end with this chapter.
Ellicott derives the word rendered rafters from a root meaning to run or flow, which yields a gutter and a curl before it yields the beams that spread overhead.
themes: a speaker the theory cannot name
a bird counted through the book
one and one are two, not three
a bed of grass and a bower of cedar
the first day of the feast ended
